summary: This unit gives you the sums a Level 3 electrician uses to plan, price and check work: Ohm's law and power, series and parallel circuits, design currents, breaker and cable choice with correction factors, voltage drop, energy costs, quantities from drawings, labour and time, and the handling of readings. You will learn to estimate before you calculate, to set out working so that others can check it, and to spot a wrong answer before it reaches the job.

blocks.p: At Level 3 you do more than follow a drawing. You work out what size of breaker and cable a load needs, whether the voltage at the far end of a run will be good enough, how much material to order, what a job will cost and how long it will take. You also check the sums of apprentices and other members of your team. A wrong figure can mean a cable that overheats, a breaker that never trips, or a job that loses money. This unit gives you the methods, and the habits, that stop those mistakes.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Collect the right figures first: the drawing and site measurements, rating plates, the specification's limits and the tables you are told to use. Decide which formula answers the question.
Use units, prefixes and rounding correctly
Change kW to W, mA to A, MΩ to Ω and mm to m without slips, and round in the safe direction for design and ordering.
Use Ohm's law and the power formulas in any form, and check an answer with a second formula or an estimate.
Solve series, parallel and mixed circuits
Find total resistance, currents and voltages, and explain why buildings are wired in parallel.
Work out loads and design currents
Add up loads from rating plates or design figures and find the current a circuit must carry, allowing for power factor and efficiency.
Apply correction factors and the rule design current ≤ breaker rating ≤ corrected cable rating; work out voltage drop and compare it with the limit.
Work with machines, transformers and batteries
Use efficiency, power factor, turns ratio, speed and frequency, and ampere-hours in everyday sums.
Take off quantities and price a job
Measure routes from scaled drawings, add drops and waste, round up to whole lengths and packs, and produce a priced list in J$ with discount and GCT.
Use worker-hours to work out days or team size, and track progress against the plan.
Work out averages, ranges, tolerance bands and percentage errors, and say whether a result passes.
Set out each sum so another person can follow it, check other people's working, and explain a mistake clearly and kindly.

ul: The JPS supply to homes and most businesses is **110 V and 220 V, single-phase, 50 Hz**. Most sums in this kit use these voltages. Larger buildings may also have a three-phase supply; three-phase sums come in later units.

Jamaica's electrical code is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**, so you will meet cable sizes in AWG (American Wire Gauge) as well as in mm², and US terms beside British ones. The methods in this kit work with either.

Money is in **J$**. General Consumption Tax (GCT) is added **at the current rate**: check the rate on the day you price a job, because it can change. Electricity rates in this kit are examples only; a real JPS bill has several charges, and they change from month to month.
Cable ratings, correction factors and resistances come from the code, the cable maker or the specification. In tests and on the job, use the table you are given, not figures from memory.

blocks.note: **Estimate first, calculate second.** Before you press a calculator key, round the figures and work out roughly what the answer should be. If the calculator then gives something very different, look for the slip. Most errors on site are not hard maths: they are a missed ×2, a kW left as kW, or a decimal point in the wrong place.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A scientific calculator (with x², √, brackets and a reciprocal key, 1/x or x⁻¹), a pencil, squared paper and the tables your instructor gives you. Learn your own calculator: they do not all handle brackets, powers of ten and negative numbers in the same way.

sections.title: Numbers, units and checking your working

blocks.p: Every electrical sum starts with figures in the right units. Most wrong answers on site come from units and rounding, not from the formula.

head: Quantity
Symbol
Unit (symbol)
Note
rows: How strongly something opposes the current.
The rate at which energy is turned into heat, light or motion.
Volts × amps. Equal to the watts only when the power factor is 1.
1 kWh is 1 kW for 1 hour, the 'unit' on an electricity bill. 1 kWh = 3 600 000 J.
Cycles per second. JPS supplies 50 Hz.
Light given out by a lamp, and light falling on each square metre.
Current × hours that a battery can supply, in theory.

head: Prefix
Symbol
Means
Example
rows: The base units: A, V, Ω, W, m

blocks.p: To change to a **smaller** unit, **multiply** (there are more of them): 0.75 kW = 750 W. To change to a **bigger** unit, **divide**: 1 250 mA = 1.25 A. Change every figure into base units (A, V, Ω, W, m) before you put it into a formula. Watch area: 1 mm² = 0.000 001 m² (10⁻⁶ m²), because a square metre is 1 000 mm × 1 000 mm.

Very large and very small numbers are written as a number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. A positive power moves the decimal point to the right; a negative power moves it to the left. 3.3 × 10³ = 3 300. 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ = 0.000 000 028. On most calculators you key the power with the EXP or ×10ˣ key, not by typing × 10 and then the power.

Calculators follow a fixed order: brackets first, then powers and roots, then × and ÷, then + and −. Keyed as 12 + 6 ÷ 2, the answer is 15, not 9. Put brackets round anything that must be done first: (12 + 6) ÷ 2 = 9. For a parallel circuit, key the whole bottom line in brackets.

ul: Keep all the figures in the calculator until the end, and round only the final answer. Rounding at every step adds errors.
Give an answer to a sensible precision: a current to 0.1 A, a voltage drop to 0.1 V, a length to the nearest 0.1 m or 10 mm, money to the nearest dollar.
In design and ordering, **round in the safe direction**, not just to the nearest figure:

head: What you are working out
Round
Why
rows: Choosing equipment for less than the real current can overload it.
Down, or keep the exact figure
Rounding up would claim the cable can carry more than it can.
Lengths, drums, packs and fixings to order
You cannot buy 5.2 lengths, and 5 would leave you short.
Rounding down makes the job late.
Number of cables allowed in a conduit or trunking
The limit must not be exceeded.
A percentage compared with a limit
3.04% must not be written as '3%' to meet a 3% limit.

blocks.p: An estimate is a rough answer you can work out in your head by rounding the figures. **Example:** a 2.7 kW kettle on 220 V. Estimate: 2 700 ÷ 200 is about 13, so expect 'roughly 12 to 14 A'. Calculator: 2 700 ÷ 220 = 12.3 A. The two agree, so the answer is probably right. If the calculator had shown 1.23 A or 123 A, the estimate would show at once that something had gone wrong.

flow: Write what you are finding and the formula
Write the figures in base units, with their units
Work it out and write the answer with its unit
Check it: an estimate, a second formula or a common-sense test
Say what it means: passes or fails, which size to choose, what to order

blocks.p: **Example.** Find the current taken by a 1.8 kW heater on 220 V. I = P ÷ V = 1 800 W ÷ 220 V = 8.18 A. Check: 1 800 ÷ 200 = 9, close enough; and 220 × 8.18 = 1 800 W. So the heater takes **about 8.2 A**.

blocks.note: Write units at every step. The commonest slips in electrical sums are: leaving kW as kW in a formula that needs W; forgetting that current goes out and back (the ×2 in voltage drop); mixing mm and m; and dividing the wrong way round. Units written beside each figure catch most of them.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Formulas and how to rearrange them

blocks.p: Most electrical sums use a small set of formulas. You must be able to use each one in any of its forms, which means rearranging (transposing) it to get the quantity you want on its own.
**V = I × R**: the voltage across a resistance equals the current through it times the resistance. Its other forms are **I = V ÷ R** and **R = V ÷ I**.

blocks.note: The triangle: write V at the top and I × R along the bottom. Cover the quantity you want. Covering V leaves I × R; covering I leaves V over R; covering R leaves V over I. The same triangle works for any formula of the form A = B × C, such as P = V × I.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Whatever you do to one side of the equals sign, do to the other side as well.
Undo each operation with its opposite: + with −, × with ÷, a square with a square root.
Undo the operations in the reverse order to the order in which they were done to the quantity you want.

head: Start with
To find
Steps
Result
rows: Multiply both sides by R, then divide both sides by P
Multiply both sides by R, then take the square root
Divide both sides by R, then take the square root
Turn both sides upside down, then multiply both sides by Np

blocks.p: All three give the same answer for the same resistor, because they all come from P = V × I and Ohm's law. That makes them useful for checking: work the answer out one way, then check it another way.

**1. A 3 kW element on 220 V.** Current: I = P ÷ V = 3 000 ÷ 220 = 13.6 A. Resistance: R = V² ÷ P = 220 × 220 ÷ 3 000 = 16.1 Ω. Check with Ohm's law: I = V ÷ R = 220 ÷ 16.13 = 13.6 A. Both methods agree.

**2. A 40 Ω load resistor must not give off more than 250 W.** What is the most current it may carry? From P = I² × R: I = √(P ÷ R) = √(250 ÷ 40) = √6.25 = **2.5 A**. Check: P = I² × R = 2.5 × 2.5 × 40 = 250 W.

**3. A 110 V lamp is rated 75 W.** Its working (hot) resistance is R = V² ÷ P = 12 100 ÷ 75 = 161 Ω. Measured cold with an ohmmeter it reads far less, because a filament's resistance rises a great deal as it heats up. Heating elements change less, but they too read a little low when cold.

blocks.note: Formulas only work in base units. A 2.4 kW heater must go in as 2 400 W. If you divide 220 by 2.4, or 2.4 by 220, the answer is wrong by a factor of 1 000, and the wrong way up as well.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Real circuits combine loads, switches and conductors in series, in parallel, or in a mixture of both. You must be able to work out the total resistance, the currents and the voltages, and use the results to check a design or find a fault.

head: Feature
Series
Parallel
rows: One after another, in a single path
Side by side: each load has its own path across the supply
Divides between the branches; the branch currents add up to the total
Divides between the parts; the part voltages add up to the supply voltage
The same across every branch: the full supply voltage
1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 … The total is always less than the smallest branch
A switch or fuse and its load; control contacts in a chain; battery cells
Lights and outlets in buildings; elements in parallel; batteries in parallel for more capacity

ul: Two resistances: R = (R1 × R2) ÷ (R1 + R2), 'product over sum'. Example: 12 Ω and 6 Ω give 72 ÷ 18 = 4 Ω.
Any number of equal resistances: R = one resistance ÷ how many there are. Four 48 Ω elements in parallel give 12 Ω.
Three or more unequal resistances: add the reciprocals, then take the reciprocal of the total. For 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 20 Ω: 0.1 + 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.2, and 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 Ω.

blocks.p: A 24 V DC supply feeds an 8 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 12 Ω and 6 Ω.

ol: Supply current: I = V ÷ R = 24 ÷ 12 = 2 A. All of it flows through the 8 Ω resistor.
Voltage across the 8 Ω: 2 × 8 = 16 V. Voltage across the pair: 2 × 4 = 8 V. Check: 16 + 8 = 24 V.
Branch currents: 8 ÷ 12 = 0.67 A and 8 ÷ 6 = 1.33 A. Check: 0.67 + 1.33 = 2 A.

blocks.p: The two checks in that example are **Kirchhoff's laws**: the current flowing into a junction equals the current flowing out, and the voltages round a loop add up to the supply voltage. Use them to check any circuit sum.

blocks.h: Why buildings are wired in parallel

ul: Every lamp and appliance gets the full supply voltage it is made for.
Each load can be switched on and off without affecting the others.
If one lamp fails, the rest keep working.
Each load added is another path, so the total resistance falls and the total current rises. That is why a circuit can be overloaded simply by plugging in more appliances.

blocks.h: Loads in series: a common mistake

blocks.p: Two 110 V appliances must not be joined in series to run them on 220 V. The voltage shares out in proportion to their resistances, so it splits evenly only if the two are identical; and even then, if one fails or is switched off, the other stops. **Example:** a 60 W and a 100 W lamp, both 110 V, in series on 220 V. Their hot resistances are 110² ÷ 60 = 202 Ω and 110² ÷ 100 = 121 Ω, 323 Ω in all. The current is 220 ÷ 323 = 0.68 A. The 60 W lamp gets about 0.68 × 202 = 137 V, well over its rating, so it glows brightly and soon fails; the 100 W lamp gets only about 83 V. (Real filaments change resistance with temperature, so the figures shift a little, but the result is the same.)

blocks.note: In a series circuit the **biggest resistance takes the biggest share of the voltage**. In a parallel circuit the **smallest resistance takes the biggest share of the current**.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Energy = power × time. With power in kilowatts and time in hours, the answer is in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)**, the 'units' on a JPS bill. **Cost = kWh × the rate per kWh.** Change minutes to hours by dividing by 60, and watts to kilowatts by dividing by 1 000.

**Example.** A 1.2 kW microwave is used for 50 minutes a day in all, every day for 30 days. Hours a day = 50 ÷ 60 = 0.833 h. Energy a day = 1.2 × 0.833 = 1.0 kWh. A month = 1.0 × 30 = 30 kWh. At J$60 per kWh (an example rate) the cost is 30 × 60 = **J$1 800**.

blocks.note: A JPS bill is made up of several charges, including a fixed customer charge, an energy charge and a fuel charge that changes each month. For estimates and audits, use the 'all-in' rate per kWh you are given, and say in your report that it is an assumption. Larger commercial customers are also billed for their maximum demand, which is one reason power factor matters to them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: No machine turns all the power it takes in into useful output; the rest is lost, mostly as heat. **Efficiency = output power ÷ input power**, as a decimal, or × 100 as a percentage. So **input = output ÷ efficiency**, and **losses = input − output**.

**Example.** A pump motor's rating plate gives 3 kW and 86% efficiency. The plate power of a motor is its **output** at the shaft. Input = 3 000 ÷ 0.86 = 3 488 W. Losses = 3 488 − 3 000 = 488 W, given off as heat in the motor.

In a heater the current rises and falls exactly in step with the voltage, and volts × amps gives the true power. In a motor, a transformer or a fitting with a magnetic ballast, part of the current only builds magnetic fields and is out of step with the voltage. Then volts × amps is bigger than the true power.

head: Quantity
Unit
How to find it
rows: What does the work and turns the energy meter. P = V × I × pf
S = V × I. Cables, breakers and transformers must carry the current that goes with this figure
pf = P ÷ S. About 1 for heaters and filament lamps; often about 0.7 to 0.9 for motors running on load

blocks.p: **Example.** An air-conditioner on 220 V takes 1 683 W at a power factor of 0.85. Apparent power S = P ÷ pf = 1 683 ÷ 0.85 = 1 980 VA. Current I = S ÷ V = 1 980 ÷ 220 = **9.0 A**. Had you used I = P ÷ V you would get 7.7 A, and might choose a cable or breaker that is too small.

**A full motor example.** A 220 V single-phase motor gives 1.1 kW at its shaft, with an efficiency of 78% and a power factor of 0.82. Input power = 1 100 ÷ 0.78 = 1 410 W. Apparent power = 1 410 ÷ 0.82 = 1 720 VA. Running current = 1 720 ÷ 220 = **7.8 A**. If the rating plate gives a current, compare: it should be close.

blocks.note: **Starting current.** An induction motor started straight on to the supply draws several times its running current for a few seconds, often about 5 to 8 times (check the maker's data). Its protection must let it start without tripping and still protect the cable: for example a breaker with a suitable tripping curve, or a motor starter with an overload relay set to the running current. Follow the motor and breaker makers' data and the designer.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: In an ideal transformer the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: **Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns** (p for primary, s for secondary). Power in is roughly equal to power out, so the currents go the other way: a step-down transformer gives a lower voltage and a higher current. **Example.** A control transformer steps 220 V down to 12 V and has 1 320 primary turns. Ns = 1 320 × 12 ÷ 220 = 72 turns. If it supplies 60 VA, the secondary current is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 A and the primary current about 60 ÷ 220 = 0.27 A (a little more in practice, because of losses).

ul: Revolutions per second = revolutions per minute ÷ 60. A machine at 1 500 rev/min turns 25 times a second.
The **synchronous speed** of an AC motor is n = 120 × f ÷ number of poles, in rev/min. On 50 Hz: 2 poles 3 000 rev/min, 4 poles 1 500 rev/min, 6 poles 1 000 rev/min.

An induction motor runs a little below synchronous speed. The difference, as a share of the synchronous speed, is the **slip**, often about 2% to 6% at full load. A 4-pole motor's plate may say 1 440 rev/min: a slip of 4%.

Equipment made for 60 Hz, common in the US, runs about one-sixth slower on Jamaica's 50 Hz, and a motor not rated for 50 Hz can overheat. Check that the rating plate says 50 Hz or 50/60 Hz before it is installed.

blocks.p: A battery's capacity in ampere-hours (Ah) is, in theory, current × hours. A 12 V, 75 Ah battery could supply 2.5 A for 75 ÷ 2.5 = 30 hours. In practice you get less: a lead-acid battery lasts much longer if it is only discharged to about half its capacity, capacity falls with age and heat, and an inverter wastes some energy. Use the maker's figure for the usable depth of discharge. **Energy stored** in watt-hours = V × Ah: 12 × 75 = 900 Wh. A 300 W load run through an inverter that is 90% efficient takes 300 ÷ 0.9 = 333 W from the battery, which is 333 ÷ 12 = 27.8 A.

The average light level on a surface, in lux, is the light reaching it in lumens divided by its area in m²: **E = Φ ÷ A**. **Example.** A classroom 8 m × 6 m = 48 m² needs an average of 300 lux on the desks. The light needed on the desks = 300 × 48 = 14 400 lm. If each fitting delivers 1 800 lm to the desks after losses, 14 400 ÷ 1 800 = 8 fittings. Real lighting designs allow for room shape, wall colours and dirt with factors from tables; the designer or the maker's software does this.

sections.title: Designing a final circuit: load, protection, cable and voltage drop

blocks.p: At Level 3 you check, and sometimes make, the calculations behind a circuit. The designer, the code or the specification sets the rules and the tables; you apply them carefully and record each step.

flow: List the loads and their ratings
Work out the design current (Ib)
Choose a breaker or fuse rating (In) at or above Ib
Find the cable's rating in the table (It)
Apply correction factors to get Iz
Check that In is no more than Iz
Work out the voltage drop and compare it with the limit
Record the working and have it checked

blocks.h: Step 1: the load and the design current

ul: From rating plates: add the watts (or VA) of the loads that can run at the same time.

From design figures: the specification or design guide may give a figure per outlet or per square metre. If a guide allows 180 VA for each general-purpose outlet in a shop, ten outlets on 110 V give 1 800 VA, and Ib = 1 800 ÷ 110 = 16.4 A.
Single-phase design current: **Ib = P ÷ (V × pf)**, or simply P ÷ V for a resistive load such as a heater.

Not every load runs at full power all the time. Designers apply **diversity** to whole installations using rules from the code or the specification. Do not invent your own diversity: use what you are given.

blocks.note: Under the NEC, on which Jamaica's code is based, a **continuous load** (one expected to run at its maximum for 3 hours or more, such as a storage water heater or the lights in a shop) may load a breaker to only 80% of its rating. Put the other way, the breaker is sized at 125% of the continuous load. Your instructor will tell you which rules the job's design follows.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The breaker or fuse rating, **In**, must be **at least the design current**, so that it does not trip in normal use. Choose the next standard size at or above Ib. Common breaker ratings include 15, 20, 30 and 40 A in NEC-style panels and 16, 20, 25, 32 and 40 A in IEC-style boards; use the sizes made for the panel on the job.

blocks.h: Step 3: the cable and its correction factors

blocks.p: A cable table gives each size's current rating, **It**, for one installation method under **standard conditions**, usually 30 °C air with the cable on its own. On a real job the cable may run through a hot roof space, be bunched with other circuits, or be covered by insulation. All of these stop it losing heat, so it can safely carry less current. **Correction factors** from the tables reduce the rating:

head: Factor
What it allows for
Typical effect
rows: Air hotter (or cooler) than the table's standard
Below 1 when it is hotter: for one common type of PVC cable, about 0.87 at 40 °C and 0.71 at 50 °C
Several loaded circuits run together in one conduit, trunking or bunch
For example about 0.80 for 2 circuits and 0.70 for 3 circuits bunched together
Cable surrounded by, or touching, thermal insulation, such as in a ceiling
Can be 0.5 or less; avoid the situation if you can

blocks.p: The factors that apply are **multiplied together**: **Iz = It × Ca × Cg × Ci**. The figures depend on the cable type and the table, so always read them from the table you are given.

**Example.** A cable rated 37 A in the table runs through a roof space at 40 °C (Ca = 0.87), bunched with two other circuits (Cg = 0.70). Iz = 37 × 0.87 × 0.70 = **22.5 A**. A 20 A breaker can protect it; a 25 A breaker cannot.

blocks.note: Roof spaces under concrete slabs and metal roofs in Jamaica often reach 40 °C to 50 °C, or more, in the afternoon. A cable sized for 30 °C can run dangerously hot there. Find out the real conditions along the whole route, and use the worst part.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz**: design current ≤ breaker rating ≤ corrected cable rating. The first part stops nuisance tripping; the second makes sure the breaker trips before the cable overheats. If In would have to be bigger than Iz, choose a bigger cable (or, if Ib allows it, a smaller breaker). **Never** fit a bigger breaker to cure tripping.

Every conductor has resistance, so some voltage is lost along it and the load gets less than the supply voltage. Too much drop makes lamps dim, makes motors run hot and struggle to start, and upsets electronics. The specification sets the limit, often about **3%** for a final circuit (3.3 V on 110 V; 6.6 V on 220 V); some designs allow up to 5% from the supply intake to the load.

**Method 1, resistance per metre.** In a single-phase circuit the current flows out on the line and back on the neutral, so the length of conductor is **twice the route length**: **Vd = I × r × 2L**, where r is the resistance of one conductor per metre and L is the route length one way.

**Method 2, mV/A/m tables.** Many cable tables give the voltage drop in millivolts per amp per metre of route, already allowing for both conductors: **Vd = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1 000**. Percentage drop = Vd ÷ supply voltage × 100.

**Example.** A 220 V circuit carries 15 A over a 45 m route. Each conductor's resistance is 0.0046 Ω per metre (given). Vd = 15 × 0.0046 × 2 × 45 = 6.21 V, and 6.21 ÷ 220 × 100 = **2.8%**: inside a 3% limit. The same load fed at 110 V would take about twice the current for the same power, and on the same cable the drop would be about 12.4 V, which is 11.3% of 110 V. That is why long runs to big loads are fed at 220 V where the equipment allows it.

head: If the voltage drop is too high
Why it works
rows: Doubling the area roughly halves the resistance, so it halves the drop.
Feed the load at 220 V instead of 110 V, if it is rated for it
Half the current for the same power, and the drop is a smaller share of a bigger voltage.
Move the panel or a sub-panel closer, or take a more direct route.
Two circuits, each carrying part of the current.

blocks.p: A conductor's resistance is **R = ρ × L ÷ A**, where ρ (rho) is the resistivity of the metal, L the length and A the cross-sectional area. For copper at 20 °C, ρ is about 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m; aluminium is about 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, so an aluminium conductor needs a bigger area to do the same job.

ul: **Length:** double the length, double the resistance.
**Area:** double the area, half the resistance.
**Temperature:** copper's resistance rises by about 0.4% for each °C. A conductor at 70 °C has about 20% more resistance than at 20 °C: R(70 °C) ≈ R(20 °C) × (1 + 0.004 × 50) = R(20 °C) × 1.2.

blocks.p: **Example.** 100 m of 2.5 mm² copper: R = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ × 100 ÷ (2.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.69 Ω. Cable tables give a little more, about 0.74 Ω, because real stranded conductors are not perfect. Use the table figure when you have one.

blocks.h: Area from diameter, and AWG sizes

blocks.p: The cross-sectional area of a round conductor is **A = π × d² ÷ 4** (the same as π × r²). A conductor 2.26 mm across: A = 3.142 × 2.26 × 2.26 ÷ 4 = 4.0 mm². For a stranded conductor use the maker's stated size: measuring across the bundle gives too big a figure.

head: AWG size
Area, about
Note
rows: The lower the AWG number, the bigger the wire.
Every 3 AWG sizes the area roughly doubles or halves.
Take ratings and resistances from the table for the cable you are using.
AWG and metric sizes are not exact matches: never swap one for the other without checking the table.

blocks.p: Cables in a conduit or trunking may fill only a set share of its inside area, so that they can be drawn in without damage and can lose heat. That share, the **fill** or **space factor**, comes from the code or the specification: the NEC, for example, allows 40% of a conduit's area for three or more conductors, and limits for trunking vary. Work out each cable's area from its **overall** diameter, including the insulation, add them up and compare the total with the allowed area. Round the number of cables **down**.

Ordering too little stops the job; ordering too much wastes the customer's money or the company's profit. A take-off (a list of quantities taken off the drawings) must be complete, checked and rounded the right way.

A drawing at 1:50 shows things at one-fiftieth of their real size: 1 mm on paper is 50 mm on site. **Real size = drawing measurement × scale number**; drawing size = real size ÷ scale number. Example: 180 mm on a 1:100 plan is 18 000 mm, which is 18 m on site.

ul: Use written dimensions where they are given. Measure (scale) the drawing only where there is no dimension, and check a known dimension first.
A copy may have been printed bigger or smaller than the original, so its written scale no longer holds. A scale bar printed on the drawing grows and shrinks with the copy, so it stays true.
Check key dimensions on site before you order: buildings are not always built exactly as drawn.

flow: Check the drawing revision, the scale and the symbol key
Count each item by type: boxes, switches, outlets, lights, fittings
Measure each route on the drawing and convert it by the scale
Add the rises and drops to each box, light and board
Add allowances for waste, bends and terminations
Round up to whole lengths, drums and packs
List everything, then have a second person check it

blocks.p: A floor plan shows routes as if seen from above. It does not show the conduit drop from the ceiling to a switch, or the rise from the floor to an outlet. Work these out from the mounting heights: with a 2.7 m ceiling and a switch centred at 1.2 m, each switch drop is about 1.5 m.

head: Item
How to work it out
rows: (Total route + drops) + a waste allowance (often 5% to 10%, as the company sets) ÷ the length of one piece; round up.
One fewer than the number of lengths joined end to end, plus any spares the company adds.
Route length × number of conductors drawn in, plus extra at each end for terminating (for example 0.3 m to 0.5 m per end, as the job needs).
Cable when runs may not be joined
Work out how many whole runs fit on one drum (round down), then how many drums the runs need (round up). The cable left on a drum may be too short to use.
Count from the drawing, add spares (for example 5% to 10%), and round up to whole packs.

blocks.p: **Example: drums.** Seven runs of 34 m are needed, with 1 m extra on each for terminating: 35 m a run. A 100 m drum holds only 2 whole runs (70 m), leaving 30 m. Seven runs need 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5, so **4 drums**. Working from the total length alone (7 × 35 = 245 m, so 2.45, rounded up to 3 drums) would leave you a run short, because the 30 m left on each drum cannot make a 35 m run without a joint.

blocks.h: Lengths that are not along a wall

blocks.p: Where a cable or tray runs straight across a room or a site, use **Pythagoras' theorem** for the right-angled triangle it makes: **c = √(a² + b²)**. Example: across a yard 9 m one way and 12 m the other, c = √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15 m. The 3-4-5 triangle and its multiples (6-8-10, 9-12-15) are worth remembering.

ul: Rectangle: length × width. A wall chase 3.2 m long and 0.05 m wide has an area of 0.16 m².
Circle: π × r², or π × d² ÷ 4.
Keep units the same: m × m gives m², and mm × mm gives mm². 1 m² = 1 000 000 mm².

blocks.note: When you are unsure whether to round up or down, ask: 'If I am wrong, what happens?' Ordering one length too many costs a little; one too few stops the job. A cable limit exceeded by one cable breaks the rule.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A Level 3 electrician prices materials, works out labour, and keeps a job on time. The sums are simple; the skill is in being complete, showing the working, and stating your assumptions.

The prices above are examples. Always use the supplier's current price list and state the date of the prices. Show the discount and GCT on separate lines so the customer can see them, and check every line: quantity × unit price = line total.

ul: x% of an amount = amount × x ÷ 100. 12% of J$85 000 = J$10 200.
One amount as a percentage of another = part ÷ whole × 100. J$30 000 of labour in a J$120 000 job is 25%.
Sharing in a ratio: add the parts, divide the total by them, then multiply. Materials to labour of 5 : 3 on a J$240 000 job: 8 parts of J$30 000, so materials J$150 000 and labour J$90 000.
Percentage increase = increase ÷ original × 100. A price rising from J$650 to J$715 has gone up by 10%.

blocks.p: Labour is measured in **worker-hours** (or worker-days): people × hours worked. Worker-hours = days × people × hours a day. Rearranged: days = worker-hours ÷ (people × hours a day), and people = worker-hours ÷ (days × hours a day). Round people and days **up**.

**Example.** A job is estimated at 120 worker-hours. Three electricians on 8-hour days need 120 ÷ (3 × 8) = 5 days. If the job must be done in 4 days: 120 ÷ (4 × 8) = 3.75, so 4 electricians are needed.
**Labour cost.** Two electricians at J$1 500 an hour and a helper at J$800 an hour, each working 40 hours: (2 × 1 500 × 40) + (800 × 40) = 120 000 + 32 000 = **J$152 000**.

Progress rate = work done ÷ time taken. Time still needed = work left ÷ rate. **Example.** A team has installed 30 of 105 lighting points in 2 days: 15 a day. The 75 left will take 75 ÷ 15 = 5 more days. If only 3 days are left, the team must reach 75 ÷ 3 = 25 points a day, so the team leader must act now (more people, longer days, or a new date agreed with the client) and not wait until the last day.

blocks.note: Estimates are only as good as the figures behind them. Keep records of how long tasks really take on your jobs, such as worker-hours per point or per board, and use them for the next estimate.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: An energy audit lists each load, its rating, how many there are and how long it runs, then works out the energy and the cost. Read the power from the rating plate. If the plate gives only volts and amps, V × A gives VA, which is more than the true watts for a motor.
Over 22 working days: 9.84 × 22 = 216.5 kWh. At J$65 per kWh (an example rate) that is about **J$14 070** a month.

**Saving and payback.** Replacing the ten 40 W fittings with 18 W LED fittings saves 22 W each, 220 W in all. Over 9 hours that is 1.98 kWh a day; over 22 days, 43.56 kWh; at J$65, about J$2 831 a month. If the LED fittings and the labour to fit them cost J$22 000, the **payback time** = cost ÷ saving a month = 22 000 ÷ 2 831 = 7.8, so **about 8 months**. After that, the saving is money in the customer's pocket.

blocks.note: Present savings in a short table (old load, new load, hours, kWh saved, J$ saved, cost, payback) and state your assumptions: the rate, the hours and the days. The customer can then check the working and see what would change the answer.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Handling readings: averages, tolerance and error

blocks.p: Tests and surveys give you sets of readings. You must summarise them, compare them with limits, and know when a reading cannot be trusted.

The **mean** (average) = the total of the readings ÷ how many there are. The **range** = the highest − the lowest. **Example.** Five continuity readings: 0.42, 0.45, 0.43, 0.44 and 0.46 Ω. Total 2.20 Ω; mean 2.20 ÷ 5 = 0.44 Ω; range 0.46 − 0.42 = 0.04 Ω.
If one reading is far from the others, do not simply average it in. Find out why: a loose test lead, a reading taken at the wrong point, or a real fault. Repeat the test and record what you found.

A **tolerance** gives the band a value may fall in and still be acceptable. **Example.** A resistor marked 220 Ω ±10%: 10% of 220 is 22, so the band is 198 Ω to 242 Ω. A 110 V supply with a tolerance of ±5% (a figure used here only as an example) may be anywhere from 104.5 V to 115.5 V. A value on the edge of the band passes; a value outside it fails.

**Percentage error = (measured value − true value) ÷ true value × 100.** A minus answer means the instrument reads low. **Example.** A meter shows 108.2 V where a calibrated reference meter shows 110.0 V: (108.2 − 110.0) ÷ 110.0 × 100 = −1.6%. Always divide by the **true** (reference) value, not by the reading.

blocks.h: When is a result close enough?

ul: Compare each result with the limit in the specification, and say clearly: pass or fail.

If a result is very close to a limit, remember the instrument's own accuracy: the true value could be on the other side of the limit. Retest with a better instrument, or report the result as doubtful.
Record readings in a table with their units, the date, the place, who took them and the instrument's serial number.

blocks.note: Never 'adjust' a reading to make it pass. A recorded result is a safety record that others will rely on. If a result fails, report it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can change between M, k, m and µ prefixes and use powers of ten.
I can round answers sensibly, and in the safe direction for design and ordering.
I can estimate an answer before I calculate it, and check it with a second method.
I can rearrange Ohm's law, the power formulas and the transformer ratio.
I can work out total resistance, currents and voltages in series, parallel and mixed circuits.
I can explain why buildings are wired in parallel, and why 110 V loads must not be put in series on 220 V.
I can work out energy in kWh and its cost.
I can use efficiency and power factor to find a motor's input power and current.
I can work out a design current and choose a breaker using Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.
I can apply correction factors to a cable rating.
I can work out voltage drop and its percentage, and suggest ways to reduce it.
I can explain how length, area and temperature change a conductor's resistance.
I can take quantities off a scaled drawing, add drops and waste, and round up correctly.
I can price a material list with discount and GCT, and work out labour cost and time.
I can work out a saving and a payback time for an energy-saving change.
I can work out a mean, a range, a tolerance band and a percentage error.
I can set out my working so another person can check it, and check someone else's.

head: To find
Formula
rows: V = I × R; I = V ÷ R; R = V ÷ I
P = V × I = I² × R = V² ÷ R
kWh = kW × hours; cost = kWh × rate
Vd = I × r × 2L, or mV/A/m × I × L ÷ 1 000; % = Vd ÷ V × 100
worker-hours = people × hours a day × days

terms: A number from a table that reduces a cable's rating for heat, grouping or insulation.
The current a circuit is expected to carry in normal use.
An allowance, set by the code or designer, for not all loads running at full power together.
A quick, rough answer used to check a calculation.
The energy used by 1 kW in 1 hour; the 'unit' on an electricity bill.
The total of a set of readings divided by how many there are.
How long a saving takes to cover the cost of the change that made it.
How far a reading is from the true value, as a percentage of the true value.
The highest reading minus the lowest.
A property of a material that sets how much a given length and area of it resist current.
The ratio between a drawing and real size, such as 1:50.
How much slower than synchronous speed an induction motor runs.
The share of a conduit's or trunking's inside area that cables may fill.
A list of quantities measured and counted from the drawings.
The band within which a value is acceptable.
Rearranging a formula to get a different quantity on its own.
The power that does work, in watts (W).
The voltage lost along the conductors of a circuit.
One person working for one hour; the unit for labour estimates.

c1.title: A water heater at an Ocho Rios guest house
c1.text: Mr Rupert Gayle, a Level 3 electrician, is adding a 220 V, 4.5 kW water heater at a guest house in Ocho Rios, St Ann, with trainee Kadeem. The cable runs 28 m (one way) from the panel, partly through a roof space that reaches about 50 °C in the afternoon. The cable chosen is rated 41 A in the table at 30 °C; the table's factor for 50 °C is 0.71, and no other factors apply. Each conductor's resistance is 0.0046 Ω per metre, and the specification allows a 3% voltage drop. For this job the designer applies the rule Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz with no other allowance.

c2.title: Pricing a pharmacy fit-out in Mandeville
c2.text: Sherine, a Level 3 electrician, is pricing the fit-out of a new pharmacy in Mandeville, Manchester. On the 1:50 drawing, the conduit route from the panel to the last outlet measures 238 mm along the walls, and the conduit then drops 1.9 m to the outlet box. Her company adds 10% to conduit for waste, and conduit comes in 3 m lengths. The labour estimate is 70 worker-hours; the pharmacy can close for only 3 working days, and the crew works 7-hour days. Her draft quotation shows materials of J$126 000 and labour of J$84 000.

c3.title: An energy audit at a Hayes basic school
c3.text: Trainees from the Centre carry out an energy audit at a basic school in Hayes, Clarendon, which is open 20 days a month. They find eight 75 W ceiling fans used 8 hours a day, and fourteen fluorescent fittings that each take 45 W (a 36 W tube plus its ballast), used 7 hours a day. The office air-conditioner's rating plate gives only 220 V and 5.2 A. The school pays about J$62 per kWh (an example rate for the audit). An 18 W LED fitting costs J$2 100, and fitting all fourteen would cost J$6 000 in labour.

c4.title: A borehole pump on an Ewarton farm
c4.text: Mr Hylton's farm in Ewarton, St Catherine, has a 220 V single-phase borehole pump. The motor's plate gives 2.2 kW output, 82% efficiency and a power factor of 0.85. A 12 V, 18 Ah lead-acid battery runs the tank alarm, which draws 0.6 A; the battery maker advises using no more than half its capacity. Mr Hylton also has a spare pump bought in the US, rated 230 V, 60 Hz, 3 450 rev/min.

c5.title: Checking an apprentice's sums in Christiana
c5.text: Mrs Simone Clarke, a Level 3 electrician in Christiana, Manchester, checks the job sheets of her apprentice, Javaun. He has written: 'Three 45 Ω elements in parallel = 135 Ω.' He checked his low-resistance meter on a 0.50 Ω reference resistor and it showed 0.47 Ω. His five continuity readings on one circuit are 0.62, 0.64, 0.61, 1.21 and 0.63 Ω, and he has written their mean, 0.74 Ω, on the test sheet.

questions.q: What is the design current of the new water heater?
o: About 40.9 A
About 20.5 A
About 48.9 A
About 990 A
questions.why: Ib = P ÷ V = 4 500 W ÷ 220 V = 20.5 A. 40.9 A comes from using 110 V, 48.9 A from dividing the wrong way (220 ÷ 4.5) and 990 A from multiplying. A quick estimate, 4 500 ÷ 200 ≈ 22 A, shows which answer is sensible.

questions.q: Which breaker rating should protect the water heater circuit?
o: 40 A: just below the cable's 41 A in the table
20 A: the standard size nearest to 20.5 A
25 A: over 20.5 A, under the corrected 29 A
32 A: the corrected 29 A rounded up to a size
questions.why: Iz = 41 × 0.71 = 29.1 A. The rule Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz needs a breaker between 20.5 A and 29.1 A, so 25 A. A 20 A breaker is below the design current and would trip in normal use; 32 A and 40 A are more than the hot cable can carry, so it could overheat without the breaker tripping.

questions.q: What is the voltage drop at the heater, and does it meet the 3% limit?
o: About 2.6 V, 1.2%: it passes easily
About 5.3 V, 4.8%: it fails
About 10.5 V, 4.8%: it fails
About 5.3 V, 2.4%: it passes
questions.why: Vd = I × r × 2L = 20.5 × 0.0046 × 56 = 5.3 V, and 5.3 ÷ 220 × 100 = 2.4%. Leaving out the return conductor halves the drop (2.6 V); dividing by 110 V instead of 220 V doubles the percentage.

questions.q: The owner then asks for a 6 kW heater on the same cable. What should Kadeem conclude?
o: Keep the 25 A breaker, because a heater cycles on and off
A bigger cable is needed: the breaker would now exceed 29 A
Fit a 32 A breaker, as it is close to the cable's 29 A rating
Nothing changes, as the voltage drop would still be under 3%
questions.why: 6 000 ÷ 220 = 27.3 A, so the breaker must be at least 27.3 A, and the next standard sizes (30 A or 32 A) are above the cable's corrected 29.1 A. The voltage drop would also rise to about 7 V (3.2%), over the limit. A 25 A breaker would be below the design current, breaking the first part of the rule.

questions.q: How many 3 m lengths of conduit should Sherine order for this run?
questions.why: 238 mm × 50 = 11.9 m, plus the 1.9 m drop = 13.8 m. Adding 10% gives 15.18 m, and 15.18 ÷ 3 = 5.06, which rounds up to 6. Rounding down to 5 leaves her short; 4 comes from leaving out the drop and the waste; 10 from reading the drawing as 1:100.

questions.q: How many electricians must work on the pharmacy to finish in the 3 days?
questions.why: People = worker-hours ÷ (days × hours a day) = 70 ÷ (3 × 7) = 3.33. Nobody can send a third of a person, and rounding down would make the job late, so 4 are needed. 10 is 70 ÷ 7 and 23 is 70 ÷ 3: each leaves out one of the figures.

questions.q: What percentage of the quotation's total before tax is labour?
questions.why: Total = 126 000 + 84 000 = J$210 000. Labour share = 84 000 ÷ 210 000 × 100 = 40%. Dividing labour by materials gives 67%, which compares the two parts instead of the part with the whole; 60% is the materials share.

questions.q: How much energy do the school's ceiling fans use in a month?
o: 4.8 kWh
12 kWh
96 kWh
questions.why: 8 × 75 W = 600 W = 0.6 kW; 0.6 kW × 8 h = 4.8 kWh a day; × 20 days = 96 kWh. 4.8 kWh is one day only, 12 kWh is one fan, and 96 000 is the answer in watt-hours, not kilowatt-hours.

questions.q: Counting both the LED fittings and the labour, about how long will the change take to pay for itself?
o: About 11 months
About 9 months
About 16 months
About 7 months
questions.why: Saving = 14 × (45 − 18) W = 378 W; × 7 h × 20 days = 52.9 kWh a month; × J$62 = J$3 281 a month. Cost = 14 × 2 100 + 6 000 = J$35 400. Payback = 35 400 ÷ 3 281 = 10.8, about 11 months. Leaving out the labour gives 9; using the 36 W tube instead of the 45 W the fitting takes gives 16; counting 30 days a month gives 7.

questions.q: A trainee writes the air-conditioner's power as 220 × 5.2 = 1 144 W. Why is this not the true power it takes while running?
o: The compressor really runs on 110 V, so the figure should be halved
The plate shows the starting current, about six times the running one
Plate figures are for 60 Hz, so they must be cut by a sixth in Jamaica
V × A is volt-amperes; below a power factor of 1, watts are less
questions.why: Volts × amps gives the apparent power in VA. A compressor motor has a power factor below 1, so its true power in watts is less: at a power factor of 0.85 it would be about 970 W. For an audit, use the watts on the plate if they are given, or measure them with a power meter.

questions.q: About what current does the borehole pump motor take when running at full load?
o: About 10.0 A
About 12.2 A
About 7.0 A
About 14.3 A
questions.why: Input = 2 200 ÷ 0.82 = 2 683 W. Apparent power = 2 683 ÷ 0.85 = 3 156 VA. Current = 3 156 ÷ 220 = 14.3 A. 10 A ignores both the efficiency and the power factor; 12.2 A ignores the power factor; 7.0 A multiplies by them instead of dividing.

questions.q: The pump's breaker sometimes trips the moment the pump starts, though the running current is well under its rating. What is the most likely reason?
o: The power factor rises to 1 for a moment as the motor starts
It draws several times its running current while starting
The motor's efficiency is too high for this type of breaker
The supply frequency doubles while the motor gets up to speed
questions.why: An induction motor started straight on line can take about 5 to 8 times its running current for a few seconds. The breaker needs a tripping curve that allows this, or the motor needs a starter with an overload set to the running current, with the cable still protected. Check the makers' data before changing anything.

questions.q: About how fast would the US pump turn on JPS's 50 Hz supply, and what else must be checked?
o: About 2 875 rev/min; check it is rated for 50 Hz
About 4 140 rev/min; check the pump can take it
3 450 rev/min: speed depends on voltage, not frequency
3 000 rev/min exactly: the 50 Hz speed for 2 poles
questions.why: An AC motor's speed is proportional to the frequency: 3 450 × 50 ÷ 60 = 2 875 rev/min, so the pump will deliver less water. A motor built only for 60 Hz can also overheat on 50 Hz at full voltage, so its plate must say 50 Hz or 50/60 Hz, or the maker must confirm it is suitable.

questions.q: For about how long can the battery run the tank alarm on its own, keeping to the maker's advice?
o: About 30 hours
About 10.8 hours
About 15 hours
About 7.5 hours
questions.why: Usable capacity = half of 18 Ah = 9 Ah. Time = 9 Ah ÷ 0.6 A = 15 hours. 30 hours uses the full capacity, which shortens a lead-acid battery's life; 10.8 comes from multiplying 18 by 0.6 instead of dividing.

questions.q: How should Mrs Clarke show Javaun that 135 Ω is wrong?
o: Parallel resistance is the average, so it is 45 Ω
In parallel the total is below 45 Ω: it is 15 Ω
Parallel resistances add, so 135 Ω is in fact right
Parallel resistances multiply, so it is 91 125 Ω
questions.why: Each element in parallel gives the current another path, so the total is always less than the smallest branch. Three equal resistances in parallel give 45 ÷ 3 = 15 Ω. Javaun has used the series rule. A quick check: a parallel answer must be smaller than every branch.

questions.q: What is the percentage error of Javaun's meter on the reference resistor?
o: +6.0%: it reads high
−6.0%: it reads low
−6.4%: it reads low
−0.03%: it is within limits
questions.why: Error = (0.47 − 0.50) ÷ 0.50 × 100 = −6.0%: the meter reads low. Dividing by the reading (0.47) instead of the true value gives 6.4%; −0.03 is the error in ohms, not a percentage. Compare the error with the maker's accuracy figure to decide whether the meter needs calibration.

questions.q: What should Mrs Clarke tell Javaun about his mean of 0.74 Ω?
o: It is correct, because one meter took all five readings
Round it to 0.7 Ω, as one decimal place is enough here
Recheck the 1.21 Ω reading before working out any mean
Record the highest reading instead, as it is the safest
questions.why: Four readings agree at about 0.62 Ω; the fifth is about twice that. It could be a loose lead, the wrong test point or a real poor joint, and averaging it in hides the problem. Retest at that point, find the cause and record what was found.

questions.q: A leakage clamp shows 0.0042 A. How is this best written on a test sheet?
o: 4.2 mA
42 mA
4.2 µA
questions.why: To change amps to milliamps, multiply by 1 000: 0.0042 × 1 000 = 4.2 mA. Writing small currents in mA avoids long strings of zeros where a slip is easy. 4.2 µA would be a thousand times smaller.

questions.q: Trunking is 75 mm × 50 mm inside, and the specification lets cables fill 45% of that area. Each cable's overall area is 13.9 mm². How many cables may go in?
questions.why: Inside area = 75 × 50 = 3 750 mm². Allowed = 3 750 × 0.45 = 1 687.5 mm². 1 687.5 ÷ 13.9 = 121.4. This is a limit, so round down to 121: a 122nd cable would break it. 270 ignores the 45% limit altogether.

questions.q: A customer has wired a 60 W and a 100 W lamp, both rated 110 V, in series across 220 V. What will happen?
o: The 60 W lamp gets about 137 V and may soon fail
Both lamps get 110 V and work normally
The 100 W lamp gets the most voltage and may fail
Neither lamp lights, as the current is far too small
questions.why: In series the bigger resistance takes the bigger share of the voltage. The 60 W lamp has the higher resistance (about 202 Ω against 121 Ω), so it gets about 137 V and the 100 W lamp only about 83 V. The voltage splits evenly only for identical loads, and 110 V loads should never be put in series on 220 V.
